title: What Minority Report got right about AI
text:
What Minority Report got right about AI

Steven Spielberg’s Precogs Are The Sharpest Portrait Of Generative AI Anyone Drew Before It Arrived — Fluent, Confident, Acting On Their Own, Hallucinations Included.

Watch Minority Report again and count what people quote from it and the answer is always the same: Tom Cruise in a black glove, waving his hands at a floating screen, conducting video like an orchestra. That image launched a thousand concept demos and a generation of gesture-controlled ambition.

It is also the least accurate thing the film predicted.

The 2002 movie, directed by Steven Spielberg and lifted from Philip K. Dick’s 1956 story The Minority Report, is remembered as a design showpiece. Look past the interface everyone copied and you find something more exact: a sketch of generative artificial intelligence.

The precogs do not look the future up in a database, they generate it by producing a fluent, confident account of what will happen, which the system treats as fact.

Swap the psychics for a language model and the machinery is identical, down to the failure the plot is built on.

That is not set dressing, it is the product specification for the tool in hundreds of millions of pockets, warning label included. The precogs were never the villains.

Read as design fiction rather than spectacle, they are the most accurate portrait of generative AI anyone drew before it arrived.

The Gesture Interface Was the Decoy

Of all the futures the film put on screen, the gesture interface is the one designers took home.

Christopher Noessel and Nathan Shedroff, who cataloged science-fiction interfaces in Make It So, describe the precog scrubber in What Sci-Fi Tells Interaction Designers About Gestural Interfaces as one of the most referenced interfaces in cinematic history. Every product person who has mimed pinch-and-swipe in a pitch owes it a royalty.

Then it aged into a gimmick.

https://medium.com/media/612c2079426ff989b7e667c5dba16011/href

Waving your arms at a vertical screen is exhausting inside a minute, and the industry had named the problem “gorilla arm” before Cruise put on the glove.

In 2010, Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen warned in Gestural Interfaces: A Step Backwards in Usability that the rush toward “natural” gestures was throwing out decades of hard-won standards — visibility, feedback, a reliable way to undo. The interfaces that won instead shrank to a slab of glass, then a voice, then a text box that answers back.

The most copied idea in the film was the one that mattered least.

Designers copy what photographs well, and a gloved hand sweeping through light is a poster while a model quietly generating a confident answer is not. So the poster got mimicked in keynote after keynote while the generative engine got built off camera.

A science-fiction interface is made to be read in two seconds, not operated for two hours — Cruise sweeps his arms because the camera needs to see him think. Believable and usable are different problems, and cinema only has to solve the first.

The same misdirection is happening again, except today the copied thing is the chat box. Change the input device all you like — glove, mouse, voice, prompt — and the hard question underneath does not move. It is what you do with an answer a machine invented and delivered without a flicker of doubt.

The Precogs Were a Generative Model

Strip the film to its plumbing and the precogs are a generative model with a homicide division. They do not retrieve a fact about the future; they synthesize one that did not exist until they generated it. Ask a language model a question and it does not look up the answer either — it generates the most plausible continuation, token by token, and hands it over with the calm authority the precogs give their visions.

For most of the film’s life that looked like fantasy. ChatGPT crossed 800 million weekly users within three years of launch, and generative models are now wired into search, email, coding tools, and the support box on half the sites you visit.

A decade ago the answer to a question was a list of links you weighed yourself; now it is one generated paragraph that has done the weighing and shows you none of it.

The precogs do not retrieve the future; they generate it, the same move that makes a language model useful and needs human in the loop.

The distinction matters more than it sounds.

  • A search engine retrieves, and when it has nothing it returns nothing — the blank is honest.
  • A generative model never returns a blank; it still produces a plausible, well-formed answer, because that is the only thing it does.

Confidence is not a signal that the system is right, it is the house style. The model gets treated as a component that returns answers, the way a database returns rows, and the difference between looking something up and making it up never comes up.

That difference is the product risk.

Josh Clark has a name for the version of this we now live inside. In Say Hello to Sentient Design, he and Veronika Kindred argue that generative interfaces are already here rather than on the way, and that we meet machine-made output dozens of times a day without registering it.

A machine producing confident answers about matters it cannot verify is now the ordinary condition.

The Precogs Were the Training Data

Now the part people find hardest to sit with. The precogs are not machines — they are three people, drugged, floating in a tank, their minds strip-mined for visions they never volunteered. Precrime’s marketing calls them a system, the state keeps them in a room the public never sees, and the apparatus rests on human beings whose contribution is compulsory and uncredited.

That is the origin question generative AI keeps trying not to answer, and the interface is exactly where the answer gets hidden.

A model’s fluency is not conjured; it is distilled from an enormous quantity of human work gathered without asking, and the bill is arriving in court. A federal judge gave final approval in 2026 to Anthropic’s $1.5 billion settlement with authors over pirated books, roughly $3,000 per work across some 500,000 works — the largest copyright recovery on record. The New York Times’ case against OpenAI heads toward trial on the same question.

The tank is not a metaphor, and every fluent answer is somebody’s labor, rendered anonymous under fair use.

It is not only the writing that got absorbed, either. TIME reported that OpenAI’s contractors in Kenya were paid between $1.32 and $2 an hour to read the worst material on the internet so ChatGPT would not repeat it.

People took the toxicity directly so the output could feel clean. The film has a precise image for that arrangement, and it is not flattering.

For designers the point is not guilt, it is disclosure. Interfaces are built to make generated output feel like it came from nowhere, and that seamlessness is a choice. Linking what the model drew on, marking which parts are retrieved and which invented — these are design decisions, and defaulting to silence about where an answer came from is the instinct that kept the tank out of sight.

The System Acts and Nobody Checks

The precogs’ visions do not sit in a report. They trigger an arrest — a team acts on the generated output before the predicted event has happened, generation and action welded together.

That weld is what the industry is racing to build, and it has a name: agents. PwC found that 79 percent of companies already have AI agents in use, tools that generate a plan and then execute it without waiting to be asked.

The dazzle is real, and so is the quiet transfer of authority, because each capability added is a decision handed to a system that generates its confidence as fluently as its answers. Every agent demo I have watched ends at the moment of success, never at someone unpicking what it did on a bad day.

The prompt box kept a person between the generated answer and the world. The agent’s whole selling point is removing them.

The prompt box kept a person between the generated answer and the world. The agent’s whole selling point is removing them.

Watch what the precrime cops do with all that automation. They do not investigate; they receive a name, confirm it on a screen, and make the arrest, with the detective work handed off to the oracle entirely. That is automation bias, the tendency to over-trust a machine and stop checking it.

A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found people defer to an AI recommendation even when it is visibly wrong, then keep making its mistakes after the system is switched off. Generative AI sharpens this, because fluency reads as competence.

Ben Shneiderman argues this is a false choice. In Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: Reliable, Safe & Trustworthy, he replaces the usual dial — more automation, less human control — with two axes and puts the goal where both run high.

Precrime sits in the opposite corner, and the rule it breaks is worth stating plainly: match the reversibility of the action to your confidence in the generation. A draft left for you to send is cheap to be wrong about, a sent email is not, a payment is less so, and an arrest is catastrophic.

The fix is not less capability but deliberate friction: show the two answers the model was torn between, and make someone type a consequential decision rather than click accept.

The Minority Report Was the Hallucination

Here is the part with the film’s name on it. A “minority report” is what happens when the precogs disagree — one generates a different outcome, and the system buries the dissent to present a single clean verdict. That suppression is the plot, and it is also a design decision. Anderton gets flagged as a future murderer, and the vision that would clear him is filed away, because the system is built to output certainty rather than doubt.

That is hallucination, described twenty years early. A generative model also discards the cloud of things it could have said and hands you one answer with the uncertainty stripped off. When that answer is wrong but fluent, it is a minority report the system declined to show you.

And it is not rare. Stanford researchers tested the legal AI tools sold specifically as grounded and hallucination-free, reporting in Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools that Lexis+ AI and Westlaw’s tool still fabricate or misstate the law between 17 and 33 percent of the time, and those are the careful, retrieval-grounded systems.

Generated prose compounds it, flattening the difference between what the model knew and what it invented, so the retrieved citation and the fabricated one sit in the same sentence.

A model confident enough to answer is confident enough to be wrong about a person.

A model confident enough to answer is confident enough to be wrong about a person. So build the minority report back in on purpose. This is not new advice — Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, published by Saleema Amershi and colleagues at Microsoft in 2019, tells you to make plain what a system can and cannot do and to support correction when it is wrong.

In practice: surface the uncertainty, show the sources beside the answer, and give the person a path to contest it before the system acts. It rarely happens because certainty ships faster than doubt, so teams round the confidence up and let the prose imply a sureness the model never earned.

Two questions cut through this on any generative feature.

  • What does it show when the model is unsure, and who absorbs the cost when it is fluently wrong?
  • If the answers are nothing and someone outside the room, you have shipped precrime with better typography.

The Real Forecast Was Never on the Screen

The film got the spectacle wrong and the substance right, which is the usual ratio for design fiction. We copied the gloves and missed the machine.

For two decades, “it’s like Minority Report” meant waving at a screen, when the truer read was the opposite — a system generating confident answers about a world it could not see, and people acting on them before anyone checked.

That future arrived, and it did not stay in the lab — It writes hundreds of millions of answers a week, drafts the email, runs the query, and increasingly acts without asking.

The edge case the film built its plot around is no longer hypothetical; it is a measured rate, aimed at people, not playlists.

The work now is not to build the generative engine; that part is done. The work is to build the minority report back into it — to treat the model’s suppressed uncertainty as a feature, not a bug, and to keep a human between the generated answer and the consequence. Watch the film again. Skip the hands. Study what the machine was so sure about, and who paid when it turned out wrong.

What Minority Report got right about AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Amelia Dimoldenberg  Reminds Us That Your Dream Job Doesn’t Have To Be Forever
text:
Amelia Dimoldenberg Reminds Us That Your Dream Job Doesn’t Have To Be Forever

After 12 years and thousands of chicken nuggets, Amelia Dimoldenberg has called time on her successful YouTube series, Chicken Shop Date.

With 3.4 million subscribers, over 1 billion views on YouTube, and 2.1 million followers on Instagram, what began as a column for Amelia’s local youth club magazine grew into one of the most popular celebrity interview formats on the press circuit.

The self-created series turned Amelia’s charming yet awkward British flirting into a compelling viral sensation and put her show at the top of every celebrity publicist’s press list.

In 2025, the host was named in Time Magazine’s TIME100 Creators list as one of the most influential digital content creators and has hosted the Academy Awards red carpet for the past three years.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Chicken Shop Date (@chickenshopdate)

On paper, the 32-year-old was at the top of her game. That’s why an Instagram post announcing the end of Chicken Shop Date came as such a surprise.

On Thursday, 3 September, Amelia wrote, “I never thought I’d stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Amelia Dimoldenberg (@ameliadimz)

Describing the show as her “very own romcom”, Amelia announced a slate of final dates before the beloved chicken shop closes forever.

While the news is sad (and we’ll all miss witnessing celebrities blush over Amelia’s signature deadpan charm), knowing when to say goodbye to a creative project is both a brave and strategic business move.

The millennial dream

As children, millennials were told they could be whatever they wanted to be. If we worked hard, applied ourselves and stayed on track, all of our dreams would come true. With elder millennials graduating into the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and zillennials graduating into a pandemic, it was also instilled in us that once you’re in the room — once you’ve “made it” — don’t ever let it go.

Exemplified by Emily Charlton’s “A million girls would kill for this job” line in Devil Wears Prada, if you were lucky enough to achieve your career dream in a climate of redundancies, cost of living pressures and stagnant wages, you should be grateful and grip onto it tightly.

But what happens when you’re ready for a new dream? For Amelia, the answer seems to be: you go for it. Through her own production company, Dimz Inc., Amelia has multiple creative opportunities in the works, including writing her own romcom film and a series in production for the BBC.

Chicken Shop Date isn’t the first example we’ve seen of a wildly successful creative project calling time while at its peak. In 2020, British pop culture podcast The High Low, hosted by writers Dolly Alderton and Pandora Sykes, called it quits after four years spent dominating the charts. The pair told Grazia UK that when they began the podcast they decided they’d be “all in” for four years.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Dolly Alderton (@dollyalderton)

“We wanted to go out on a high, and we feel like we’ve really honored the show by ending it now,” they told journalist Anna Silverman. Since ending The High Low, Dolly has gone on to publish her novel Good Material in 2023, write a Pride and Prejudice Netflix adaptation, and turn her memoir, Everything I Know About Love, into a TV series.

Pandora has created the UK’s number one culture newsletter, Books+Bits, and hosted multiple podcasts, including The Missing and Unreal: A Critical History of Reality TV for the BBC.

While the pair have gone on to work on other exciting things, there’s no denying that walking away from a creative and commercially successful project is daunting.

In a capitalist society, where success is measured by wealth and, increasingly, social media views, “quitting” a successful venture rejects the sunk-cost fallacy. But perhaps our idea of success should be ever-changing. We’re constantly told to dream bigger, but maybe the bravest thing you can do is admit that you’ve already achieved the dream — and start a new one.

I’m reminded of this as I sit in my therapist’s office explaining that the people I once aspired to work with are now my creative peers. How it’s so normal. The therapist suggests that, despite having achieved exactly what 24-year-old me wanted, maybe six years on I’m a bit… bored. Maybe, for this chapter, I’ve “made it”. She asks what a new dream could look like. It feels like a revolutionary statement, but she’s right. What was The Dream in your early 20s doesn’t have to be the same at 30.

Our culture teaches us to always strive for more: more money, more followers, more opportunities. But as Amelia has shown, it can be even more satisfying to close a chapter on your own terms rather than continuing on until the format stales or, as the internet is wont to do, Amelia gets “woman’d” (a phrase coined by culture writer Rayne Fisher-Quann for the cultural phenomenon where the internet stops liking a woman at the same time).

In a recent interview with Rolling Stone, Canadian musician Sarah McLachlan explained why she ended her music festival Lilith Fair after just three years. Between directing a festival, touring, songwriting, and recording albums, similar to Amelia, Sarah made a call on when to step back from a successful project.

“I like ending things on a high note,” Sarah shared. “It was also a selfishly motivated thing too, of ‘I’m sort of losing myself’ in this too much.”

It’s a sentiment Amelia seems to understand. With a movie and TV series already in the works, we know that the Chicken Shop Date host will go on to achieve other markers of traditional Hollywood success. But there’s no denying that it’s refreshing to see a woman create her own bootstrapped series, turn it into a cultural phenomenon, and then decide that this particular dream has run its course — even while it’s still at the top.

title: Uranus Retrograde In Gemini Is Here — & It’ll Be A Transformative Moment For You
text:
Uranus Retrograde In Gemini Is Here — & It’ll Be A Transformative Moment For You

Cosmic beings, take note because the yearly backward spin of Uranus has been in full gear for nearly five months now. From September 10th, 2026, to February 8th, 2027, the retrograde is going to challenge us in many ways, but mostly give us the power to march on and become the best versions of ourselves. Uranus in Gemini is teaching us to use our voice to speak up. We get to take command of the narrative and make our own rules to follow.

title: Your Horoscope This Week: September 6 To 12
text:
Your Horoscope This Week: September 6 To 12

Cosmic beings, the second half of this week turns the volume up, but thankfully the cosmos gives us both intensity and perspective at the same time. Venus enters Scorpio on September 10th, making love, money, beauty, desire, and attachment feel much deeper and more magnetic than they have lately. We may want more honesty, more loyalty, more chemistry, and a little less small talk, but this energy can also make us more obsessive, possessive, or emotionally reactive if we’re feeling insecure. Mercury enters Libra that same day and helps cool things down by bringing more diplomacy, balance, and fairness to the way we communicate. So even if your feelings are loud, your words don’t have to be reckless. Let yourself feel deeply, but give the conversation enough space to stay constructive.

Also on September 10th, Uranus begins its five-month retrograde in Gemini, asking us to look back at the changes in mindset, communication, technology, and daily information overload that have been unfolding since Uranus first entered this sign. Then, late that night, the Virgo New Moon arrives and officially closes eclipse season, which feels like finally being handed the steering wheel again after weeks of cosmic plot twists. This is the first time in over a month that intention-setting feels especially supportive, but keep it simple. Choose the one or two shifts that’d make your life cleaner, healthier, more organized, or more sustainable over the next six months, and build from there. Less is more this week, especially when the goal is creating a life you can actually maintain.

Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, how does it feel to realize that magnetism works better when you stop chasing everything at full speed? Venus enters Scorpio this week and moves through your intimacy, merging, shared-resources, and soulmate realm, making your connections feel deeper, more magnetic, and much harder to keep casual. You may feel more drawn to someone, more willing to talk about money or vulnerability, or more aware of who actually has access to your energy. Financially, this can also bring support through a partner, client, investment, or outside resource. Just watch the urge to obsess over every signal or read seventeen layers into one text. If the connection is real, it can handle directness.

Then the Virgo New Moon arrives on September 10th in your health, work, and routine zone, giving you a clean post-eclipse reset around how you actually live day to day. As much as you enjoy momentum, this fresh start works best when you slow down enough to notice where your energy has been leaking through bad habits, overbooking, or trying to do too much at once. Pick one or two routines that would genuinely make your life easier over the next six months and commit to them without turning it into a military operation. Eclipse season already rearranged enough furniture; this week’s New Moon is about deciding where everything should actually go.

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, this week turns up the volume in your relationship world, and pretending you’re unbothered may require more acting than usual. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your partnership and soulmate realm, making one-on-one connections feel more magnetic, intimate, and revealing. You may feel more drawn to someone, more interested in deepening an existing relationship, or more aware of where reciprocity has been missing. This is excellent for honesty, chemistry, and meaningful bonding, but watch the tendency to become possessive, suspicious, or overly attached to getting a specific response. Let people show you who they are without interrogating every pause between texts.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your creativity, romance, fate, and inner child zone, giving you one of the sweeter post-eclipse resets of the zodiac. You don’t need to reinvent your whole life this week; you need to remember what makes you feel alive enough to want to participate in it. Start the project, go on the date, return to the hobby, or make space for more beauty and play in your schedule. Virgo energy helps you turn inspiration into something sustainable, so choose the joy you can actually keep making room for instead of waiting for some dramatic life overhaul to deliver it.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, this week could make your daily life feel a little more intense than usual, especially around work, wellness, and the people you interact with on a regular basis. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your health and routine realm, making you much more aware of what feels supportive versus what quietly drains you. You may become more invested in improving your habits, your work environment, or even the way you care for your body, but there can also be a tendency to obsess over getting everything “right.” If you notice yourself turning one imperfect day into a full existential review of your life choices, that’s probably your cue to zoom out. Small adjustments will go much further than trying to micromanage yourself into perfection.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your home, family, and emotional foundation zone, offering a fresh start after weeks of eclipse-season movement. You may suddenly feel called to make your space calmer, spend more time with family, rethink where you want to live, or have a conversation that creates more peace behind closed doors. If you find yourself wanting to reorganize your home or pull back socially for a few days, that’s probably this New Moon helping you create a stronger inner foundation. You don’t need to solve your entire family history this week; simply making home feel more supportive of who you are now is enough.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, this week pulls you deeper into the people and experiences that actually make life feel worth living. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your romance, creativity, fate, and inner child realm, making attraction stronger, emotions richer, and your desire for meaningful connection much harder to ignore. A crush can intensify, an existing relationship may feel more passionate, or a creative idea could suddenly become something you care about on a much deeper level. Just be mindful of turning chemistry into certainty too quickly. Scorpio energy loves depth, but it can also convince you that one meaningful moment must automatically mean forever.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your communication, learning, and local community zone, giving you a cleaner slate mentally after eclipse season. Don’t be surprised if you suddenly feel ready to have a conversation you’ve been avoiding, organize your thoughts more clearly, or finally put structure around an idea that has been floating around for weeks. This New Moon favors precision over noise, so the more intentional you are with what you say, write, or commit to, the easier it becomes to create momentum without overwhelming yourself.

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, this week makes home, family, and your private emotional world feel a lot more magnetic and a lot harder to ignore. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your roots and domestic realm, deepening your desire for privacy, intimacy, and a space that actually feels emotionally nourishing. You may become more protective of your home, more invested in a family relationship, or more drawn to making your environment feel beautiful and secure. There can also be some old family intensity bubbling up, so try not to let one loaded comment turn dinner into a season finale.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your money, security, and self-worth zone, offering a practical reset after the drama and acceleration of eclipse season. You may suddenly feel more motivated to tighten your spending, rethink what you’re charging, or create a clearer plan for how you want your finances to look over the next six months. This New Moon works best when the goal is simple and sustainable, so focus on the one financial shift that would make you feel noticeably more secure rather than trying to become a completely different person by Friday.

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Virgo, this week brings more depth to the way you communicate, connect, and process what people are really saying beneath the surface. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your communication and local community realm, making conversations more intimate, magnetic, and emotionally revealing. You may feel more drawn to meaningful exchanges, writing, reconnecting with someone nearby, or saying what you actually feel instead of keeping everything perfectly edited. Just watch the tendency to overanalyze tone, subtext, or one oddly punctuated message as if it contains a secret code.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th takes place in your sign, giving you one of the clearest personal reset points of the season. After eclipse season moved so much around you, this is a chance to come back to your own body, priorities, identity, and sense of direction without trying to reinvent yourself overnight. You may feel called to refresh your appearance, change your routines, or make one decision that better reflects who you are now. The strongest move is the one that feels simple enough to sustain and meaningful enough to actually change your life.

Libra Sun & Rising:

Libra, this week makes money, self-worth, and what you truly value feel a lot more personal. Venus, your ruler, enters Scorpio and moves through your income and security realm, deepening your relationship with money and making you more aware of what feels worth your time, effort, and energy. You may feel more motivated to save, earn, invest in yourself, or become clearer about where your resources are going, but Scorpio energy can also bring scarcity fears or comparison to the surface. Try not to let one expensive week convince you that your entire financial future is doomed. Use the intensity to get more honest about what you want to build.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your spirituality, solitude, and closure zone, giving you a quieter reset after eclipse season. You may feel a stronger need to pull back, sleep more, journal, pray, or simply spend less time absorbing everyone else’s energy. This New Moon is less about announcing a dramatic new beginning and more about clearing enough internal space for your next chapter to actually fit. The most important shift may be private, subtle, and completely invisible to everyone except you.

Scorpio Sun & Rising:

Scorpio, this week puts your magnetism front and center, and people may be picking up on your energy before you even say much. Venus enters your sign, making you more attractive, more selective, and more aware of what you actually want in love, money, beauty, and pleasure. You may feel like refreshing your look, leaning into a more sensual side of yourself, or becoming much less interested in lukewarm connections that require you to decode every mixed signal. The upside is confidence and deeper connection; the shadow is becoming so intense about what you want that you start trying to control the outcome. Let yourself be desired without turning the experience into a psychological case study.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your friendship, community, and future-goals realm, offering a clean reset around who you want beside you in your next chapter. You may feel ready to reconnect with certain people, become more intentional about your online presence, or finally give structure to a long-term dream that has been floating around in your head. This New Moon favors quality over quantity, so the shift may be as simple as choosing a smaller circle that feels more aligned or committing to one collaborative goal that can actually grow over the next six months.

Sagittarius Sun & Rising:

Sag, this week makes your inner world feel richer, more private, and a little harder to brush off with a joke. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious realm, which can deepen your dreams, intuition, romantic fantasies, and need for emotional privacy. You may feel more nostalgic, more reflective about a past connection, or more drawn to creating beauty behind the scenes rather than performing for anyone. Just be careful not to romanticize what already showed you its limits. Scorpio energy can make memories feel cinematic, but that does not automatically make them a sequel.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your career, reputation, and long-term goals zone, giving you a practical reset around what success actually looks like now. You may feel called to simplify a professional plan, tighten your strategy, or become more intentional about one goal that deserves your full attention over the next six months. Rather than chasing ten different possibilities at once, this New Moon helps you notice which path has the strongest foundation beneath it. The clearer you become about what you are building, the easier it will be to stop wasting energy on opportunities that only look impressive from far away.

Capricorn Sun & Rising:

Capricorn, this week turns up the intensity in your friendships, communities, and long- term goals, especially where loyalty and shared ambition are concerned. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your social network realm, making certain connections feel more meaningful, magnetic, and potentially useful for where you’re headed next. You may feel drawn toward a new collaboration, become closer with someone in your circle, or realize that a friendship has more emotional depth than you initially thought. At the same time, you may become more selective about who gets access to your plans. Everyone doesn’t need the full blueprint, and Scorpio energy is very comfortable with a little strategic privacy.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your travel, education, publishing, and expansion zone, giving you a fresh start around how much bigger you’re willing to think. You may suddenly feel ready to revisit a course, plan a trip, apply for something, teach what you know, or commit more seriously to a vision that has been sitting in the background. This New Moon rewards practical ambition, so the best next step may be less glamorous than the dream itself, but far more useful. Once the first real piece is in place, the rest of the path becomes easier to see.

Aquarius, this week makes your career, reputation, and public image feel more magnetic, strategic, and impossible to treat casually. Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your professional realm, which can draw more attention to your work, deepen an important connection with a boss or client, or make you more intentional about the image you project publicly. You may feel ready to refine your brand, pursue a role with more influence, or become more selective about which opportunities are actually worth attaching your name to. Scorpio energy can also make you hyperaware of power dynamics, so try not to assume every closed-door conversation is secretly about you.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your intimacy, shared-resources, and transformation zone, giving you a chance to reset the way you handle trust, money, debt, and emotional merging after eclipse season. A financial agreement may need clearer terms, a relationship may be ready for deeper honesty, or you may simply realize that certain entanglements have become more complicated than they need to be. This New Moon favors thoughtful restructuring, so the shift may come through one practical decision that gives you more clarity, more reciprocity, and less psychic clutter over the next six months.

Pisces Sun & Rising:

Venus enters Scorpio and moves through your travel, education, spirituality, and publishing realm, making you more magnetic in spaces that stretch you beyond the familiar. You may feel more drawn to travel, study, teach, create, or connect with someone from a different background, and romance can feel especially intense when there’s a sense of mystery or adventure involved. Just be mindful of idealizing the journey so much that you ignore the practical details. Scorpio energy loves depth, but even soul-searching benefits from checking the return flight.

Then the Virgo New Moon on September 10th activates your partnership sector, oﬀering a fresh start in love, friendship, collaboration, and the way you relate one-on- one. You may feel ready to define a relationship more clearly, have a practical conversation about expectations, or become more discerning about who gets close to you in the first place. After eclipse season, this New Moon helps you approach partnership with less fantasy and more intention, which can actually make connection feel safer and more fulfilling. The next six months are less about forcing certainty and more about building bonds that can hold both tenderness and reality.

title: Serious Question: Is Full Coverage Foundation Dead?
text:
Serious Question: Is Full Coverage Foundation Dead?

My earliest memories of shopping for foundation and concealer were largely shaped by what I saw in the pages of teen magazines and YouTube beauty guru tutorials. I remember words like “cover,” “mask,” and “hide” being used to describe what complexion products were supposed to do. At the time, it resonated deeply: I had severe acne across most of my face, and I was specifically looking for a product that would hide as much of my skin as possible and temporarily give me the smooth, even complexion I was chasing.

That was more than a decade ago, and a lot has changed: My adult breakouts are much more manageable, and my makeup collection is bursting at the seams with a product that barely existed in the 2010s: skin tints.

These lightweight, skincare-meets-makeup formulas impart a sheer veil of coverage — essentially the opposite of what I was looking for during those early days of wandering drugstore aisles. But I can’t help but wonder if I’m not alone in feeling like my makeup sensibility has evolved, too. Which brings me to the question: What does that mean for full-coverage foundation?

In a world enamored with blurred-but-not-completely-covered complexions, the full-coverage face beat can feel like a relic of another era. But that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re ready to abandon coverage altogether. “I definitely think people are wanting their skin to look and feel more like skin — [and] for me, that’s always been the goal,” celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips tells Refinery29. “My clients want their complexion to feel perfected, but they still want to see their real skin coming through.” 

So is full coverage actually on its way out? I asked several makeup artists what’s replacing it — and whether less really is more. 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Which products are replacing full-coverage foundation?

It’s not just lightweight skin tints and sheer foundations. Buildable, medium-to-full-coverage formulas have gotten remarkably good, too, with finishes that are increasingly undetectable and skin-like.

“I’ve always believed beautiful complexion isn’t about covering everything or making the skin look perfect; it’s about putting product where you need it and letting the rest of the skin come through,” says Phillips. “That’s exactly what I wanted when creating m.ph Le Skin Foundation, something weightless and skin-like that you can apply in a thin layer, but still build where you want more coverage.”

Other editor-beloved options include Drunk Elephant’s new Kamo Drops, which can be mixed into moisturizer or worn alone for customizable coverage, and e.l.f. Cosmetics’ Soft Glam Foundation, which retails for $8 and creates a demi-matte, blurred finish that lends an airbrushed effect while still allowing my natural texture and tone to peek through.

“There’s also something very modern about being able to see real skin,” says makeup artist and Ciele founder Nikki DeRoest. “A little texture or a freckle coming through makes makeup feel alive and personal rather than overly perfected.”

In other words, you don’t necessarily have to choose between a bare-faced look and a traditional full beat. Today’s complexion products make it easier to land somewhere in between — or change your mind halfway through getting ready.

DashDividers_1_500x100

What techniques are worth trying?

Brushes, sponges, clean fingers…there’s no shortage of debate over the superior tool for base makeup application. But when it comes to making fuller coverage look as undetectable as possible, technique can be just as important as the formula.

One trick I swear by is “priming” your brush (a technique made popular by makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes): Dot your foundation onto the back of your hand, then work it into the bristles before applying it to your face. This helps distribute the product more evenly and prevents you from depositing a concentrated layer of foundation in one spot.

Phillips agrees that a lighter hand can make all the difference. “It’s less about covering everything and more about being really intentional with where you’re placing product and how much you’re using,” she explains. “I always start with thin layers and build only where I need it. You can always add more, but you don’t necessarily need the same amount of coverage everywhere.”

Another option: Pair your favorite skin tint with concealer to create a complexion that looks more covered without requiring a full layer of foundation. “I like to start with a thin layer of Enhancing Tint to even out the complexion and create that beautiful, seamless base,” explains makeup artist Lisa Eldridge. “Then I’ll add [concealer] coverage only where I need it. My Pinpoint Concealer is fantastic for this because you can be incredibly precise, rather than covering the entire face.”

The takeaway? If you love a full-coverage foundation, you don’t have to give it up — just start using it a different way, like concentrating it where you actually want more coverage, and leaving other areas lighter or even bare. The result can still be a perfected complexion — just one with a little more dimension.

DashDividers_1_500x100

What’s the future of full coverage makeup?

Eldridge agrees: “I think our idea of ‘flawless’ skin has definitely changed,” says Eldridge. “I don’t think it has to mean completely poreless, completely matte, or completely uniform anymore: Beautiful skin has dimension. It has texture, freckles, little variations in color and all of those things that make it look real.”

In other words, think of skin as not just one step with one product; “What I think has changed is the idea that coverage has to be all or nothing,” says DeRoest. “We’re becoming much more comfortable customizing it: sheer here, medium there, concealer exactly where it’s needed. The modern complexion is really about having control over your coverage and letting your skin still feel like your skin.”

And perhaps that’s the real answer to whether full-coverage foundation is “dead.” Not exactly. The bigger shift is that we’re no longer treating coverage as an all-or-nothing proposition. You can want to cover a breakout, even out discoloration, blur texture, or simply wear a full beat because you like the way it looks — and none of those choices necessarily have to mean covering every inch of your face.

title: 17 Revamped Haircut Trends Dominating Fall, According To Top Stylists
text:
17 Revamped Haircut Trends Dominating Fall, According To Top Stylists

Okay, we aren’t exactly lacking in haircut trends. Recently, we fell for the “curve” cut — a strategically layered style that adds major volume to fine strands — and then we spotted the J-shape haircut, with its loose layers that fall effortlessly into that rounded silhouette. But with a shiny new season comes a fresh wave of haircut ideas.

Whether you’re eyeing the “cloud” bob or craving something shorter, like a pixie crop, there’s a trend for everyone.

Ahead, top hairstylists from London to NYC share the cuts set to define fall — and beyond.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Varsity Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by steph hui (@stxph.h)

Hair artist Tom Smith describes the varsity bob as a choppy, chin-skimming cut with subtle layers and a center part. The inspo? Steph Hui and Millie Bobby Brown. “Polished but never prissy, it carries a cool collegiate energy — youthful without being childish and preppy without being stiff,” says Smith. While the movement might look undone, it’s actually intentional and well-maintained, adds Smith, thanks to the invisible layers through the mid-lengths and ends that create that flicky volume.

Gucci Bangs

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Dimitris Giannetos (@dimitrishair)

“Gucci bangs feel very fashion-forward — and powerful,” says celebrity hairstylist and colorist, Dimitris Giannetos. He recalls creating the softly-parted, slightly grown-out look for Demi Moore ahead of her role as the fictional character Barbara Gucci in the short film The Tiger. “To achieve this look, ask for wispy curtain bangs just below the brows with face-framing pieces towards the ears,” recommends Giannetos. The key? “Avoid a blunt cut by adding some variety to the length of the bangs across the face,” he says.

The Clean Cut Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Deborah Iona | Beauty & Lifestyle (@deborahiona)

“Anok Yai’s striking short bob, complete with a blunt fringe, highlights the boldness of this style,” says celebrity hairdresser Lorraine Dublin. “It’s a sharp, chin-skimming bob paired with a clean fringe, and it’s set to stand out this [fall].” Why? It has a strong, modern silhouette, Dublin explains, yet still feels polished and low-maintenance. We also love the look on content creator Deborah Iona.

The Ripped Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Catherine Gibbs (@ccatherinee.g)

Nick Stenson, celebrity hairstylist and founder of Nick Stenson Beauty, highlights the “ripped” bob as the standout cut of fall 2026. “Bobs are making a comeback because their clean, structured shape offers a chic, low-maintenance look that pairs perfectly with cold-weather layers,” says Stenson. The ripped bob, however, is a more interesting, layered take, thanks to softly separated ends created with a texturizing technique where the hair is chopped into vertically. This cut by Catherine Gibbs is perfect.

The Feathered Shag

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by ✧✧ 𝕽𝖄𝕰𝕹𝕹𝕰 𝕾𝕹𝕺𝖂 ✧✧ (@ryennesnow.hair)

The shag is set to take on a much gentler image this fall, according to Neale Rodger, style director at STIL salon in London. “Think soft, feathered layers that build volume and create easy movement,” says Rodger, like this look by Ryenne Snow. Rodger adds that it’s the kind of cut that still looks intentional even as it grows out. “It’s a brilliant choice for medium to thick hair,” continues Rodger, “especially if there’s already some natural wave or texture to play with.” Guiding your stylist is simple: “Ask for feathered layers throughout, soft ends, and a length that sits somewhere between the neck and shoulders,” advises Rodger.

’60s Bangs

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by ✧✧ 𝕽𝖄𝕰𝕹𝕹𝕰 𝕾𝕹𝕺𝖂 ✧✧ (@ryennesnow.hair)

The ’70s have had their time in the sun. Now, it’s 1960’s time to shine, and bangs are leading the resurgence, says Ricky Walters, founder and creative director of Salon 64. “The new incarnation is all about boldness: think thick, heavy, statement-making fringes taken surprisingly far back into the crown,” says Walters. He adds, “This isn’t a whisper of a fringe; it’s a full-volume curtain that instantly reshapes the face, adding drama, mystery, and a touch of French-girl rebellion.” Walters says that cutting it with plenty of density — adding bulk through techniques like point cutting and texturizing — prevents it from slipping into anything too dated. Hairstylist Ryenne Snow always nails it.

The Power Pixie

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Iris Law 🧼🧊 (@lirisaw)

The power pixie has Florence Pugh, Glenn Close, and Iris Law to thank for its meteoric rise. “This is a cropped, layered pixie that’s sharp, sculpted, and deliberately androgynous,” says Smith. Its key characteristics? “Enough length and the top and front to allow for versatile styling,” adds Smith, who calls it the ultimate anti-blowout style. “This is great for finer hair types and those who want more lift, as it helps to contour the jawline and cheekbones when long enough to be tucked behind the ears,” says Smith. Asking for it couldn’t be simpler: “Ask for close layering and texture that can shift from matte and punkish by day to polished and glossy at night,” advises Smith — and don’t forget the longer, swooping bangs.

The Bubble Cut Blowout

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Dimitris Giannetos (@dimitrishair)

The name sounds complicated, but the result speaks for itself. It’s essentially a soft blowout with rounded, bouncy ends, explains Giannetos, who recently debuted the look on Amal Clooney. “It works well on long, layered hair, about 6-8 inches from the shoulder. This look enhances body, adds movement, and makes the blowout feel thicker and more voluminous,” says Giannetos. “I like to take a 1.25” Bio Ionic Curler to the ends to lock in the rounded shape.”

The Polished Pixie

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SIA | Lifestyle • Outfits • Beauty (@sialuxe_)

Super-short styles are still trending, says Dublin, but the polished pixie is having a moment. Just look to content creator Sia. “It’s perfect if you want a low-maintenance cut that holds up through the colder, wetter months,” Dublin says, adding, “If you’re not ready for a full chop, a pixie-style wig gives you the same look with zero commitment.”

The Shaggy Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Akesha Reid (@keeksreid)

The shaggy bob is not only effortlessly chic, says Dublin, but it’s practical for winter and spring. “The layers add movement and texture — great under scarves or hats — while still looking polished for work or evening plans,” adds Dublin. Grab a hydrating hair cream like PATTERN by Tracee Ellis Ross Palo Santo Styling Cream and let your natural texture do its thing. This cut on Keeks Reid is beautiful. 

The Modern Shag

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SHAG! (@shaglondon)

Mussed-up texture is in this season, says Stenson, and while the classic shag’s layering technique is making a comeback, it’s being reimagined for fall with modern softness and volume. “Even better, it’s flexible across hair types,” he adds. “A shag is great for anyone with thick hair because it removes weight and bulk. If you have finer hair, ask for a modern micro-shag or wolf-shag with strategic layering that adds volume and texture without making the hair look sparse,” advises Stenson. This cut on Linasha never fails to inspire. 

The Shaggy Lob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Catherine Gibbs (@ccatherinee.g)

“The textured lob [aka long bob] will continue its quiet takeover,” says Rodger. “It’s mid-length, slightly undone, and effortlessly cool — the kind of cut that behaves beautifully through winter,” he adds. It’s also a seasonal all-rounder, and easy to air-dry in the warmer months, too. “I love how it slips under scarves and coats without losing shape, and it gives hair that natural, lived-in movement,” continues Rodger, who says it’s perfect for wavy and lightly curly hair. “Ask your stylist for a neck-to-shoulder graze with feathered, textured ends, and a soft, natural finish,” suggests Rodger. Hairstylist Catherine Gibbs nails the look here.

The One-Length Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by miho mai / 福岡ボブ / ボブ / ボブパーマ / 福岡美容室 / ナチュラル (@zoey__mai)

The fall update is lighter than its previous counterpart, says Walters, and it sits in what he refers to as the magic zone: “Just above the collarbone and never shorter than the jawline,” adds Walters, like this cut by Miho Mai. “This sweet spot creates a clean, graphic silhouette without sacrificing softness.” What gives it a modern edge is the invisible layering: “These are subtle, sliced-in shorter pieces hidden underneath,” says Walters. “These secret layers act like built-in movement, allowing the bob to swing, breathe, and catch the light in all the right ways.”

Curtain Bangs 2.0

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Charlotte | Macomb MI Hairstylist (@charlottexstyles)

If they’re not cut properly, curtain bangs can look blocky and unnatural, failing to blend into the rest of your lengths. That’s why Stenson suggests asking for “texturized” curtain bangs. Texturized bangs are cut with techniques that soften the fringe and remove bulk, so they fall more naturally. “Your stylist will assess the density of your hair to ensure your bangs are proportionate to your face,” says Stenson. “Bangs are especially a great choice for those with fine or thin hair and looking to bring some volume to their look. They’re truly versatile enough to suit all face shapes.” Take inspiration from this cut by @charlottexstyles on Instagram.

The Chin-Length Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Dimitris Giannetos (@dimitrishair)

Gianettos says that there’s something so chic about a sharp bob that grazes the chin and that it can elevate any outfit. “It feels very confident, effortless, cool-girl,” says Giannetos. “It can be worn wavy for an everyday style or straight for a very sleek, edgy look,” — much like this cut on Meredith Duxbury. “I like to use L’Oreal Paris’ Sleek It Iron Straight Hairspray to tame any frizz that distracts from the moment,” says Giannetos.

The Bixie Cut

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 𝕮𝖍𝖊𝖑𝖑𝖘𝖎𝖊 𝕶𝖎𝖌𝖊𝖗 𝕾𝖊𝖗𝖗𝖆𝖓𝖔 (@chellsiedanielle)

The bixie — bob meets pixie — is heading into fall with us, and for good reason: it’s soft, wearable, and short enough to feel fresh, says Rodger. “This is a sweet spot between a bob and a pixie, and it’s ideal for anyone tempted to go shorter without committing to a full pixie,” says Rodger. He adds that it works especially well on fine to medium hair, which always benefits from added texture through the mid-lengths and ends. “When you’re asking for it in the chair, think chin length or slightly above, with light, choppy layers and a soft, airy finish.” We love this crop by Chellsie Aiger Serrano.

The Blunt Bob

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by abbie de fontaine (@abigaillilydefontaine)

Rodger is convinced that a “clean, blunt bob” is the answer to feeling polished without the effort, like this cut on STIL client Abbie de Fontaine. “The strong, even line gives you instant structure,” he says. “Plus, it looks incredible peeking out from under winter and spring layers.” He adds that the cut is particularly beautiful on slightly wavy or straight, finer hair, as it lends weight and sharpness. For the best result, Rodger suggests asking for a chin-to-collarbone bob with crisp, blunt ends and minimal layering. “Keep it sleek or lightly textured depending on your hair type,” he says.

title: When Endometriosis Makes My Body Unrecognizable, Perfume Helps Me Reclaim It
text:
When Endometriosis Makes My Body Unrecognizable, Perfume Helps Me Reclaim It

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

Some mornings, it feels like my body has been awake for hours before I have. By the time I catch up, it’s already made a series of executive decisions. I’ll stand in front of my closet wondering why nothing feels right, only to realize it’s not the clothes, but the body wearing them. Yesterday’s jeans suddenly feel optimistic; the dress I’d planned to wear belongs to a version of myself who didn’t show up today. After changing twice, I accept the outfit was never the problem. 

Overnight, there’s a heaviness that wasn’t there before. Bloating has appeared from nowhere, and the kind of fatigue sleep barely touches. That’s the strange thing about endometriosis — a condition where cells similar to those lining the uterus grow elsewhere in the body, causing severe pain among other debilitating symptoms. Not only does it change how your body feels, but it changes your relationship with it. Alongside the agony, the fatigue and hormonal shifts mean I’m constantly being reintroduced to my own body. 

That’s usually the point where I do something that sounds faintly ridiculous until you’ve lived it: I reach for perfume.  

The women finding comfort in scent 

While it doesn’t fix anything, fragrance is one of the few things I still get to choose before my body starts calling the shots. More often than not, it’s Esteè Lauder Bronze Goddess — mine and my mom’s summer scent. It smells like vacations, warm, salty skin, and the version of me that existed before pain became something I had to factor into every plan. I wear it because it reminds me I’m still in there somewhere. 

You see, endometriosis erodes the certainty of knowing myself until my body no longer feels like somewhere I can reliably come home to. So when everything else feels unpredictable, is it any wonder I reach for something that smells like continuity? As it turns out, I’m far from the only person with a chronic illness who’s turned my love of fragrance into something much bigger than a simple spritz. 

For Rioco Green 32, fragrance offers a brief escape when her endometriosis flare-ups make the world feel painfully small. “Scent has an amazing ability to transport you somewhere else,” she tells me. Her ritual begins with Aesop Geranium Leaf Body Oil, a herby, invigorating, and grounding scent that helps her momentarily disconnect from the pain while making her feel as though she’s actively caring for a body that’s asking so much of her. 

For Amie Flynn, 34, wearing perfume is about recognition. During an endometriosis flare-up right before a work meeting, she recalls standing in front of the mirror thinking, This isn’t me; it’s just my symptoms. She reached for Jo Malone Poppy & Barley Cologne, as she always does. “The familiar fragrance gave me a moment to pause and reset,” she tells me. “Instead of focusing on how unwell I felt, I was reminded of who I am beyond my diagnosis.”  

None of us expect perfume to perform miracles. Instead, we all ask remarkably little of it: to remind us of who we were before our symptoms got there first. 

Why perfume is more than just beauty — & the science behind it 

Dr. Sula Windgassen, a health psychologist specializing in chronic illness, says this response is remarkably common: “[With endometriosis], body image can be affected by swollen bellies, confidence reduced by brain fog, and your sense of meaning or value as a person can be obscured by pain. It can feel like you just need to survive,” she says. In this version of life, Dr. Windgassen points out something that makes complete sense to me: “Even these small acts of choice start to carry more weight.” 

I recognize this more than I’d like to admit, even when choosing a perfume starts to feel like a personality trait I’m clinging to. It’s where scent slips beyond beauty altogether. Dr. Windgassen adds, “Routines, bodily states, work and relationships can all shift with chronic illness […], but scent can act as a stable cue when everything else is in flux.” 

There’s also a more scientific side to it. Dr. Windgassen points out that certain scents — most notably lavender, bergamot, and chamomile — can activate the parasympathetic nervous system: “This is the body’s built-in ‘calm down’ setting,” she explains. “It slows heart rate and reduces stress responses before you’ve even had time to talk yourself out of it.” 

Unlike other senses like taste or touch, smell doesn’t go through the brain’s usual editing process. “It goes almost directly from the nose to the olfactory bulb, the amygdala, and the hippocampus — areas responsible for emotion and memory,” explains Dr. Windgassen. That could explain why on the hardest days, something as simple as wearing a fragrance during an endometriosis flare-up can offer a little respite. 

How scent can become a grounding ritual for living with endometriosis

It’s something I know all too well. Choosing a perfume on my most painful days is one of the few things my body and I can still agree on. After speaking to psychologists, I kept coming back to one word: anchor. Not in a poetic, lifestyle sense, but something more literal — a way of not drifting too far from myself. 

This is something Anishka Sooriah, 25, has also experienced. She describes losing herself after endometriosis surgery to remove the tissue growing outside of her uterus. For Sooriah, scent became something entirely archival: “There’s this oud oil that my partner gifted me,” she recalls. “Whenever I wear it now, it pulls me straight back to those early days of the relationship. I miss that version of myself sometimes, before the pain.” 

While the emotional pull of scent is deeply personal, there’s also science behind why certain fragrances can make us feel more like ourselves. Dr. Anna Persaud, a biochemist and CEO of This Works, where fragrance meets wellness, says that while we often think of fragrance as purely aesthetic, it can provide emotional support. “Because fragrance engages both memory and emotion simultaneously, a familiar scent can create an immediate sense of recognition and continuity,” she says, adding, “It becomes a sensory cue that reconnects us with ourselves.” 

During periods of grief, upheaval and illness, Dr. Persaud explains that people often return to fragrances they’ve worn for years because familiarity can do the emotional heavy lifting. “Scent doesn’t just help us remember those experiences,” she explains. “It can help us re-experience some of the [positive] emotions associated with them.” Let’s not get it twisted; the perfume isn’t transporting you elsewhere. Instead, it’s a reminder that you’re still here. 

Chriselle Lim, founder of Phlur, has noticed that this shift is now influencing purchasing behaviors. “People are wearing fragrances for themselves rather than other people,” she tells me, adding, “Choosing and applying a scent creates a small sense of normalcy and control.” Lim suggests choosing by mood — and there’s a knack to it. Citrus notes, for example, are thought to boost energy, while skin-like musks feel cocooning and comforting, and woody notes have a grounding effect.  

On my shelf, that means Kilian Paris Sunkissed Goddess (ylang ylang and coconut) for extra warmth, Diptyque Fleur de Peau (bergamot and musk) when I need wrapping up a little, Phlur Paradise Nectar (mandarin and pink pepper) to lift my mood, and Miu Miu Fleur de Lait (mango, coconut, and osmanthus flower) on the days I want to borrow some confidence.  

How I use perfume to find my way back to myself

Naturally, my body decided this would be the week to fact-check everything I’ve just said, and I’m in the middle of one of the worst endometriosis flare-ups I’ve had in months. I’ll spend the next five to nine days cancelling plans, measuring time in pain instead of calendars, and missing the woman I was a few days ago.  

Perfume won’t change any of that. It won’t calm the inflammation, shrink the bloating, or give me back the energy that this condition steals. It isn’t a treatment, and it certainly isn’t a cure. But tomorrow morning, before I face another day of this flare, I’ll still reach for the Bronze Goddess. Not because I want to smell nice, but because, for a few seconds, it reminds me that this version of me isn’t the whole story.  

I used to think perfume was the finishing touch. Turns out, on the days I need it most, it’s where I begin.

title: The Case Against Saving Your Favorite Perfume “For Best”
text:
The Case Against Saving Your Favorite Perfume “For Best”

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

I’ve spent most of my life believing that beautiful things were not meant for ordinary days. Growing up working-class, anything that felt like a luxury came with a quiet set of rules: You looked after it. You made it last. You didn’t use it up too quickly, because replacing it wasn’t always an option. As such, a favorite jumper was saved for occasions; a new pair of shoes was kept box-fresh for as long as possible. And perfume — especially perfume — was something to be rationed.

​The bottles I received for birthdays were some of the most special things I owned. They felt grown-up and extravagant, a little glimpse into a life where I could buy things I loved without worrying about the cost. But because they were so precious, every spray became a decision. I used to think: Was today really worth using it?

Then my aunt died.

While clearing out her belongings, we opened her wardrobe and found bottles of her favorite perfumes: Cacharel Anaïs Anaïs and Nina Ricci L’Air du Temps — all unopened, waiting.

I can’t explain exactly why that sight affected me so much. On the surface, they were just bottles of fragrance, but they represented something much bigger: all of the little pleasures we postpone while waiting for a day that feels more worthy — the celebrations we imagine are coming or the version of ourselves that finally deserves to use the “good” things.

My mom looked at those untouched bottles and said something I’ve never forgotten: “You see, this is why you should never save anything. Wear everything, as it matters — like it’s your last day. Even if it’s just for going to the store. You love it, so you wear it.”

That last sentence has stayed with me ever since, because the more I thought about those unopened bottles, the more I realized my aunt’s perfume wasn’t just about fragrance — it was about all the things we put off enjoying until we believe we’ve earned them. Since then, I’ve found myself questioning why we are so quick to save things that bring us joy. Why does a favorite perfume feel too special for Monday morning? Why do we wait for birthdays, holidays, and big occasions before allowing ourselves to enjoy something we already love?

Jessie Wilner, founder of Discothèque fragrances, helped me put it into words: “We’re conditioned to save [things] for important occasions because modern life is modeled around these supposedly seismic events,” she tells me. Sure enough, friends say they have bottles they only wear for weddings, anniversaries, or vacations. One admitted she’d owned the same expensive bottle for years because she was saving it for something “important.” Another said she kept hers in its original box so it would stay as “pristine” as possible. My sister-in-law has a Diptyque Figuier candle she was given for her 30th birthday that she still hasn’t lit. Whenever I ask why, she just says, “It’s too good to light.”

Likewise, I used to fiercely guard my birthday perfume with my life. One year, it was Prada Paradoxe — all tangerine, jasmine, and warm musk — sprayed so sparingly I almost counted every spritz. The next year: Issey Miyake L’Eau d’Issey, with its watery lotus, fresh lilies, and soft woods; then Estée Lauder Bronze Goddess, with creamy coconut, tiare flower, and vanilla. Each one felt like proof that I had been given something extravagant, and I treated it accordingly: special outfits, special plans, special moods only. But this, says Wilner, means we forget to romanticize the condition of existence. In an increasingly tough world, that matters more than ever.

I understand the thought process. Maybe it comes from growing up without much to spare or the way we’re taught to protect expensive things, to preserve luxury, to keep them untouched for a moment that feels important enough. When money is tight, using something luxurious can feel oddly irresponsible, as if every spray needs to be justified. Even now, with what I think of as “adult money”, I still catch myself calculating whether my Christian Dior Bois Talisman or Diptyque Orpheon is worth wearing for a supermarket trip or a day spent working from home. 

Elodie Durande, perfumer at Ffern, thinks many of us have been conditioned to believe expensive things should only be enjoyed occasionally. The idea of treating perfume as something precious goes back generations. Historically, fragrance was used in religious practices and as a marker of wealth and status. While perfume has become more commercialized, it’s still often treated as something to be saved. “Perfume is such a luxury item, and there’s only a finite amount that comes in a bottle,” Durande tells me. Sure enough, Scento reports that luxury perfume prices rose sharply globally between 2020 and 2025, with raw materials, marketing, and packaging all contributing to higher costs. If you can afford these luxuries, though, Durande says that they deserve to live in the present: “To get the best of them, you need to use them, and enjoy the experience.”

She also raised something I hadn’t considered: the notion that pleasure must be earned. “I think sometimes we feel we need to work to deserve life’s luxuries,” she says, but she also asks, “If you’re always saving something special for when you go out, are you wearing it for others [or] for yourself?”

That question lingered long after the conversation ended. I realized I’d been saving perfume for the moment I felt most presentable and impressive; working from home had only made it easier to convince myself there was no point wearing it at all. But as Wilner says, “Scents are just another way to connect with yourself and others. They don’t have to mark the moments that matter; they can be part of what makes them matter.” Left untouched on a shelf, it’s just liquid in a glass. Worn on an ordinary morning, though, it becomes part of a memory, a mood, and a version of yourself moving through the day.

Sarah Reason, perfume enthusiast and founder of curated fragrance store Soliflore, tells me she sees this realization in customers all the time: “The right moment is today,” she says. “We can’t predict tomorrow, and there’s no guarantee a special occasion will come along that feels worthy enough. If a fragrance makes you feel confident, comforted, or simply happy, then that’s reason enough to wear it.” The joy comes from wearing it, not collecting it, says Reason, which is the exact opposite of the mindset I’d grown up with, but one I’m learning to embrace.

Eudora Nwasike, a certified fragrance specialist and content creator, arrived at the same conclusion through a much more personal experience. After her father passed away in 2022, she talks about one of the greatest lessons he left her with — to never wait for a special occasion. “Every waking day counts as a special occasion, because nothing in life is promised,” she tells me. “Don’t deny yourself little pockets of joy in a rough world. Wear your fragrances, expensive or affordable.” Her favorites include Amouage Purpose Eau de Parfum, plus the more affordable Zara Fashionably London Elixir Parfum and Phlur Cherry Stem Eau de Parfum, to name a few.

Certainly, there’s some science behind those little pockets of joy, too. One recent study found that pleasant fragrances may boost positive emotions and improve social interactions. Another study found that certain scents, such as lavender and ylang-ylang, could enhance mental performance and focus. With that in mind, ​my Jo Malone Sea Salt & Bergamot Cologne now sees the grocery store aisles. Discothèque’s Baise Moi on The Dancefloor comes with me on dog walks. Acqua di Parma Rosa Nobile has accepted that each spritz now includes emails, errands, and occasionally standing in the kitchen wondering what to make for dinner.

So I’ll leave you with a very small act of rebellion: I’m no longer saving anything for best. Now, every spritz of the fragrance I own feels like a small act of gratitude, a reminder to use what I love while I’m here to enjoy it. Perhaps that’s the lesson my aunt taught me without ever knowing it: the things we love aren’t meant to be preserved for a life that hasn’t happened yet. They’re meant to be part of the one we have now.
